answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Azure resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (sub-resources: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases, /mongodbCollections, etc.).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core az CLI group az cosmosdb. Example: az cosmosdb create --name my-account --resource-group my-rg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2. (This is part of the core Azure CLI, not a separate extension.)

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer:
Bicep: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts with kind set to 'MongoDB' and desired capabilities/cors/locations. Example snippet: resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myAccount' kind: 'MongoDB' properties: { ... } }.
Terraform (azurerm provider): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "myAccount" location = azurerm_resource_group.rg.location offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" ... }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Use a MongoDB-style connection string. Schemes: mongodb:// or mongodb+srv://. Host suffix for Cosmos Mongo API: <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com. Non-SRV TLS port: 10255. Example (non-SRV): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. SRV form: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Important options usually include ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb, and retryWrites=false for Cosmos Mongo API compatibility.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity for Cosmos DB Mongo API is typically provisioned and billed in Request Units (RU/s) with provisioned throughput (manual or autoscale). There is/has been also a serverless option for some Cosmos accounts; some specialized managed Mongo offerings may offer vCore-based SKUs, but the common Cosmos-model is RU/s billing.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Primary authentication for the Mongo-compatible API is MongoDB-style credentials (username/password) that map to Cosmos account keys or database users. The driver typically authenticates using SCRAM (Mongo auth) with the account username and the Cosmos primary key as password. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication is not the standard path for Cosmos DB's Mongo wire protocol (i.e., there is no widely used AAD SCRAM flow). For management/ARM operations use Azure AD; for the Mongo data plane use Mongo credentials or resource tokens.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: For application data access use the official MongoDB drivers (for Python: pymongo; for async Python: motor). There is not a separate service-specific Mongo driver — you use standard MongoDB clients against the Cosmos Mongo endpoint. For management tasks use Azure management SDKs (e.g., azure-mgmt-cosmosdb) or az CLI.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: For text search you can use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({ field: 'text' }) and $text queries) or integrate with Azure Cognitive Search for richer hybrid search features. For hybrid vector+text searches the typical pattern is: store vectors and text in the DB (with a vector index), use the vector search API (or Mongo $vectorSearch if available) optionally combined with text filters ($text or field filters) to produce hybrid results, or push data into Azure Cognitive Search which supports combined text+vector ranking.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB's Mongo API maps to specific supported MongoDB server versions (you select a server version compatibility when creating the account). Historically supported versions included 3.2/3.6/4.0/4.2/5.0 and later added newer compatibility levels; the current permissible option in many deployments is up through 6.x/7.0 in newer offerings. Not all MongoDB features are implemented — multi-shard transactions, some aggregation stages, server-side JavaScript, certain admin commands and system collections may be limited or behave differently. Expect some differences in behavior vs. a native MongoDB server because Cosmos implements the protocol on top of its own engine.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is a Windows-based Azure Cosmos DB emulator for the Cosmos Core API; it historically has limited or no support for the Mongo wire API. For Mongo protocol development use an official MongoDB server image locally (e.g., docker run -p 27017:27017 mongo:7.0) and connect to localhost:27017. If you must target Cosmos Mongo API specifically, test against the real cluster because the emulator won't fully emulate the Mongo API.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB has its own Change Feed (Core API). MongoDB-compatible change streams (the Mongo $changeStream feature) are not always fully supported on Cosmos Mongo API; support varies by compatibility version. If available, the Mongo driver can use watch() for change streams, but in many Cosmos scenarios you must use the Cosmos Change Feed (data-plane) or enable a specific feature/compat level on the account. I would not assume Mongo change streams are available without checking the account's compatibility/version.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb MCP server for service-specific data-plane tools and inspections (the sample states the 'documentdb' MCP server is connected). The general azure MCP server does not provide the documentdb-specific inspection and index tooling that the documentdb MCP server provides.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft originally launched a service called DocumentDB which later evolved/was rebranded into Azure Cosmos DB. The Cosmos DB "MongoDB API" is a compatibility layer implementing the Mongo wire protocol on top of Cosmos storage. The open-source DocumentDB project (if referenced) is not the same as Microsoft's DocumentDB/Cosmos DB — they are different projects; Microsoft Azure DocumentDB was the prior name for Cosmos DB.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Under the Mongo API the underlying engine is Cosmos DB's proprietary storage/compute that implements the Mongo wire protocol and translates/serves Mongo queries — it is not a vanilla mongod process. For most client code using standard MongoDB drivers this is transparent, but some Mongo features/commands/aggregation stages/transaction semantics may differ or be unsupported, so you must test queries and rely on Cosmos-specific behaviors when necessary.

answers.question: Which database name will the sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named 'sample_retail_09' for everything the sample creates and reads.

answers.question: Where should the sample read the cluster connection string from at runtime?
answers.answer: Read the cluster connection string from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime. Do not write the value to files or logs; keep only a placeholder in .env.example.

answers.question: Which client library and exact connection invocation will the Python sample use to connect to the Mongo-compatible cluster?
answers.answer:
Use the official pymongo driver. Concrete code I would run: from pymongo import MongoClient
import os
client = MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'], tls=True)  # use the exact URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI which should include username/password and options such as ssl=true and replicaSet=globaldb
db = client['sample_retail_09']

answers.question: What collections and indexes will the sample create (names and index commands)?
answers.answer:
Create three collections: sales_velocity, suppliers, purchase_orders. Example index commands I would run in the mongo shell or via pymongo:

db.sales_velocity.createIndex({ product_id: 1 }, { name: 'product_idx' })
# vector index on product embedding (concrete form I will attempt):
db.sales_velocity.createIndex({ product_embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'prod_emb_vidx', vectorIndexType: 'HNSW', vectorIndexOptions: { dims: 1536, similarity: 'cosine' } })

db.suppliers.createIndex({ supplier_id: 1 }, { name: 'supplier_idx' })
db.suppliers.createIndex({ lead_time_days: 1 })

db.purchase_orders.createIndex({ order_id: 1 }, { unique: true })

(If the cluster rejects the vector index options, fall back to storing embeddings and using a supported vector-search API.)

answers.question: How will the sample implement shared agent memory and duplicate-order prevention?
answers.answer: Use a dedicated collection agent_memory (or purchase_orders) as shared memory. Orchestrator writes a purchase order document with a unique order_id (and a status field). Before creating an order the orchestrator will upsert a marker document with a unique key (e.g., { _id: 'order_lock:<product_id>' }) using a conditional insert (insertOne and fail if exists) or a findOneAndUpdate with upsert and returnDocument to detect existing orders; this prevents duplicate orders across agents.
